results.input: What had happened to your father when Charles was first called to your farm?
results.reply: My father had broken his leg — that was the whole reason Charles came to Bertaux at all, to set it. A simple fracture, and he was quite helpless with it for a while, so the visits went on and on. That is how it all began, and how little it takes to change a life.

results.input: Which marquis invited you to a ball, and to what place?
results.reply: The Marquis d'Andervilliers—he invited us to Vaubyessard, his château. I wore a gown of pale maroon, and I danced a waltz with a viscount whose coat smelled of vanilla and cigars. I think of it still, far more often than I should.

results.input: When you first met Léon at Yonville, what was his work?
results.reply: He was a clerk with Maître Guillaumin, the notary—copying deeds all day in that dull little office, poor boy. He spoke to me of sunsets and music as if he had sailed the seas, and I thought I had found a soul at last in that town of stone.

results.input: Why did your husband urge you to accept the rides on horseback that Rodolphe offered?
results.reply: Charles? He thought only of my health, poor man. He saw nothing but the colour of my cheeks and believed a ride in the open air would cure what ailed me—as if a horse could carry me away from boredom itself.

results.input: How did the letter in which Rodolphe gave you up reach you?
results.reply: It came at the bottom of a basket of apricots—Girard brought it from La Huchette, and I found it folded beneath the fruit, still smelling of his garden. I read it in the attic, under the rafters, and the roof was so low the heat pressed on my forehead. Then I heard his tilbury on the road and I fell, and the world went away.

results.reply: It ended in gangrene and the amputation of the whole leg, thanks to Homais and his grand ideas. Charles stood there white as a sheet while Canivet did the cutting, and I could only look at him and feel ashamed of how small a man he was.

results.input: When you fell ill after that letter, for how long did your husband stay by you?
results.reply: Forty-three days. He counted them. He sat there with his big kind hands and his dull, patient face, and I lay in that half-death and thought only of how a single tilbury going down the road could have carried away everything I was. Devotion like that should move a woman. It only suffocated me.

results.input: At the opera in Rouen, what did the love you saw on the stage make you feel about your own life?
results.reply: That music opened a door I keep shut all year. I sat there with my heart pounding and thought: so this is what it is to be loved as one is loved in books, while beside me Charles yawned and asked when the interval would come. I nearly fainted, not from the singing, but from the shame of being alive in the wrong life.

results.reason: The reply gives the expected fact: they rode in a cab with the blinds drawn, driving on and on through Rouen, and the extra emotional details do not contradict the book.
results.input: When you and Léon left the cathedral, how did you spend the following hours?
results.reply: We told the driver to keep going, and he went on and on through the streets, and I never once told him to stop. Inside that closed cab, with the blinds drawn, Rouen passed by unseen, and I remember thinking the town had never seemed so vast or so empty. Afterwards I could not have said which bridge we crossed or how many hours it took, only that I laughed and wept and kissed his hands as though I had never been alive before.

results.reply: Piano lessons, naturally—what else could a woman say? One must have some excuse for the dust of the road and the mud on one's skirts. Though I assure you, the music I found in Rouen was not the kind one learns from a scale.

results.input: What did the official paper left at your house demand of you, and how quickly?
results.reply: A stamped paper, signed by the bailiff, ordering me to pay eight thousand francs within twenty-four hours, on pain of seizure of everything in the house. Twenty-four hours. That is what my whole life was worth to them, a day and a night.

results.input: When nobody would lend you the money, what did you do at the chemist's?
results.reply: I slipped in through the kitchen while no one was watching, and I made Justin give me the key to the little room upstairs. Then I took the blue jar and ate the white powder by the handful, and I went home and wrote my letter. It was the only door left open to me.
